stateNote: The droplet is not paid for yet. Everything on this page is the setup this site is built to run on, and the deploy path is already committed to the repo: the Dockerfile, the compose files and the Coolify guide are what would go up, not a sketch of what might. When the box exists this file gets one field changed and the page starts reporting measured numbers instead of intended ones.

host.note: The $6 tier has 1 GB and does run a single small Next.js container, but Coolify builds on the box, and a Next.js build inside 1 GB needs swap and still gets killed often enough to be miserable. The $12 tier is the honest number for this setup.

services.name: portfolio
services.purpose: This site. Next.js standalone output on Node 22 alpine.

services.name: coolify
services.purpose: The deploy layer. Watches GitHub, builds the image on the droplet, swaps the container, keeps the previous one until the new one answers.

services.name: coolify-proxy
services.purpose: Reverse proxy and TLS. Coolify manages it, certificates come from Let us Encrypt on first request for a hostname.

services.name: uptime-kuma
services.purpose: Monitoring. Probes this site and every deployed project on a schedule, keeps the history, and exposes a public status page.

services.name: postgres
services.purpose: Shared database for the projects that need one, so each app is not paying for its own managed instance.

pipeline.detail: Push to main on GitHub. Nothing else on my machine is involved.
GitHub calls the Coolify webhook on the droplet.
Multi-stage build on the box: deps, then build, then a runner stage carrying only the standalone output and the static assets.
Coolify starts the new container and waits for it to answer before it touches the running one.
Traefik is pointed at the new container. The old one is stopped, not deleted, so a rollback is one click.
Uptime Kuma notices the restart, records it, and the response time on this page is measured against the new container from then on.

monitoring.note: Self-hosted rather than Healthchecks.io because the whole argument of this page is that I run the thing myself. The status page is public when the droplet is up. Until then the response times below are measured live from this site rather than read from a monitor, which is a weaker claim and is labelled as one.

targets.name: GitHub Pages
